articles.title_orig: SNAP's funding model is starting to change. Here's what that means for the program
articles.title_zh: SNAP's funding model is starting to change. Here's what that means for the program
articles.content_orig:
A customer shops for produce in an H-E-B grocery store in Austin, Texas, on May 11. Brandon Bell/Getty Images hide caption
The Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) is undergoing a drastic restructuring of its funding model — one that will reduce federal support and require states to shoulder a larger share of the bill.
Historically, the federal government and states have evenly split the food aid program's operational costs, such as paying for state workers and training staff. But starting on Thursday, states will need to cover 75% of that tab while federal funding shrinks by half.
By the federal government's own calculations , the new rule will lead to a $16.9 billion reduction in federal spending for SNAP over the next five years, or $3.4 billion annually.
The Food Research & Action Center, an anti-hunger advocacy group, estimates that states would need to shore up anywhere between $3 million and $670 million to fully offset the loss in federal funding for administrative costs. California, New York, Pennsylvania, Texas and Michigan are expected to be especially hard hit.
Over the past year, states have been rebalancing their budgets to account for the new costs. But they will likely need to tighten their belts even further as more funding changes are on the horizon.
Currently, food benefits are covered entirely by federal dollars. But starting in October 2027, states may have to pay for a portion of the food aid if their error rate — a measure of overpayments and underpayments to SNAP recipients — is at or above 6%.
The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a left-leaning think tank, estimates that nearly half of states could each pay $100 million or more if they do not lower their error rates. California and New York could each be on the hook for over $1 billion if they are unable to do so, according to the think tank.
In a report published last year, the Georgetown Center on Poverty and Inequality estimated that these changes together will force states to spend two to three times more to keep the food assistance program running.
These mounting costs will put states in a bind, where they will likely have to find new sources of revenue, cut funding from other programs or further restrict access to SNAP, according to Katie Bergh, a senior policy analyst with the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities.
"And we may see some states decide that they need to withdraw from the program entirely," Bergh says.
The funding changes were triggered by President Trump's signature domestic policy law, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which was enacted in July 2025. The White House said the legislation preserves and strengthens the food assistance program, adding that it was "so bloated that it is leaving fewer resources for those who truly need help."
But Bergh says SNAP's previous funding structure served a purpose.
"That essentially ensured that eligible families who were seeking benefits could get them even if they lived in a state that had much higher rates of poverty or a smaller tax base," she says.
The Agriculture Department, which administers SNAP, has not yet responded to a request for comment.
The One Big Beautiful Bill Act also introduced other sweeping changes, adding stricter work requirements and ending food aid eligibility for the small pool of noncitizens who previously qualified.
Since Trump's second term began, the number of people receiving SNAP benefits dropped from 42 million to 36 million, as of June. Most of that decline happened after the One Big Beautiful Bill was signed into law.

articles.title_orig: ‘These guys are in a pickle’: Some Republicans spurn Trump on the campaign trail
articles.title_zh: ‘These guys are in a pickle’: Some Republicans spurn Trump on the campaign trail
articles.content_orig:
Welcome to From the Politics Desk , a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.
In today’s edition, senior national political reporter Sahil Kapur looks at how Trump is reacting to Republicans putting some distance between themselves and the White House before the midterms. Plus, senior reporter Alexander Smith digs into a big issue in European politics with some echoes in recent U.S. politics — links between domestic right-wing parties and Russia.
With President Donald Trump ‘s approval rating dipping and voters turning toward Democrats ahead of the 2026 midterm elections, numerous Republican candidates have sought to distance themselves from him — scrubbing him from their websites , using their voices or votes to disapprove of the Iran war , and more.
For the most part, Trump has let it slide, in some cases downplaying the political signaling by wary allies to his skeptics in the electorate.
But not in the case of Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar , the three-term Florida Republican who represents a Miami-area district. Last week, she ran a straight-to-camera ad , filmed outside the White House, condemning Trump’s immigration agenda.
“Mr. President, some of your immigration enforcement efforts have gone too far,” she says in the ad, pointing at the camera and adding that “the same Hispanics who helped you get to the White House in 2024 feel betrayed today.”
Salazar has reason to be worried, even though she won her last two elections by double digits and Trump handily carried her district in 2024. The district is 74% Hispanic.
Between 2020 and 2024, Trump made double-digit gains with Hispanic voters nationwide, according to exit polls. But his ratings have fallen precipitously since then. In the latest NBC News poll, Latino voters disapproved of Trump by 2 to 1.
Other Republicans have cause for concern, too. Trump’s national approval rating is 39% in the NBC News polling average (or about 20 points underwater), falling from 50% (or about 5 points above water) when his second term began. Against that backdrop, Republican candidates have sought some distance on Iran, gas prices and other issues in recent weeks.
But it was Salazar who faced the brunt of Trump’s ire.
Over the weekend, the president went on Truth Social to repost more than a dozen social media posts slamming Salazar. “She’s openly pro-amnesty,” said one commenter reposted by Trump. “She tried a stunt and it backfired!” wrote another. “She is nothing but a back stabber,” wrote yet another. “Trump must remove his endorsement from her,” said a fourth. A fifth commenter boosted by Trump called for replacing her with a “new” Republican.
It serves as a warning shot to other Republicans not to cross the line or he’ll put them on blast with his base of supporters, whom the GOP needs to turn out to vote in November.
Less clear is where the line is. Salazar’s direct and public confrontation on TV — which has long been Trump’s preferred media — ran afoul of it.
But Florida governor candidate Byron Donalds , who has removed mentions of Trump from his website, did not violate his red line; Trump downplayed his distancing on social media.
Neither did Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks , R-Iowa, who voted two weeks ago for a Democratic-led resolution to end the Iran war, or Rep. Ashley Hinson , R-Iowa, who last week said the war should end.
On Monday, Trump hosted Iowa lawmakers, including Miller-Meeks and Hinson, in the Oval Office to announce a new steel plant in Iowa. “We’re going to do a great rally. We’ll all be there together. We have to get you all elected,” Trump said. “We’ll save you a good Iowa pork chop, sir,” Hinson chimed in.
Europe’s far-right parties are on the rise , seemingly well positioned to ride a groundswell of anti-establishment sentiment into power in several countries in the next few years.
But as anxiety mounts over threats of sabotage and cyberattacks from Russia , the resurgent right is facing scrutiny over past ties to the Kremlin — and questions about how it might approach Moscow in the future.
A striking pivot came this month from French far-right figurehead Marine Le Pen , the front-runner in next year’s presidential election.
In a joint statement with Jordan Bardella , another key figure within her National Rally party , Le Pen said she would “never tolerate” Russia using “intimidation, threats, destabilization or psychological pressure” to influence French policy.
They also condemned Moscow’s seizure of French and other European companies’ assets as “a hostile act against the interests of France and the nations of Europe” that “must be firmly condemned.”
It’s a notable rhetorical evolution from Le Pen, who only a few years ago was declaring her admiration for Russian President Vladimir Putin , playing down threats from Moscow and facing intense scrutiny over a 9.4 million-euro ($10.7 million) loan to her party from a Russian bank.

by AMAC — The Association of Mature American Citizens
Photo: Justin Sullivan/Getty Images
Most of the leftist excesses of COVID-19 have fallen by the wayside, and mail-in voting is no exception. With the pandemic's politics fading from view, more voters are choosing to vote the old-fashioned wayâin person, at a polling booth.
For half a decade, the Democratic Party treated mail-in voting as sacred. It met any suggestion that elections require a trip to the polls as an attempt to kill grandma with COVID-19 or disenfranchise car-less widows. Even reasonable requests, like ballots that include a voter's driver's license or Social Security number, Democrats have attacked as an attempt to suppress minorities and the poor.
But as with forced masking, lockdowns, vaccine requirements, and remote learning, this too doth pass.
In 2020, about 46 percent of voters cast ballots by mail. This included 58 percent of Democrats and 33 percent of Republicans, according to Pew Research Center's study of validated voters. That pattern has faded. A new NBC News poll finds that 69 percent of registered voters now plan to vote in person and only 21 percent plan to vote by mail.
The poll shows that among Democrats, 72 percent plan to vote in personâsplit evenly between early voting and Election Day. Only 23 percent plan to vote by mail, down from 34 percent two years ago and far below 2020 levels. Five percent are unsure if they will vote at all.
Independents are moving the same way. Twenty-eight percent plan to vote early in person, up six points from 2024, and 20 percent plan to vote by mail, down from 28 percent in 2024.
Republicans recovered from COVID-19 brainrot by 2024 and are the only group that shows no change in its voting pattern since then. Over half plan to vote in person on Election Day, and 16 percent plan to vote by mail.
There are inherent risks to mail-in voting. Depending on the state, these include automatic registration, chain-of-custody challenges, delayed counts, andâoften fraudulentâballot harvesting. Those who recognize these risks understand the surest way to reduce the possibility of fraud is to restrict mail-in voting as much as possible. It would be preferable for Congress to lock in the way most states handled it before COVID-19: needs-based absentee voting.
The House of Representatives passed the Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE America) Act, which would require proof of citizenship to vote by mail. Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-MO) introduced an amendment to that bill that would restrict mail-in voting to needs-based cases, such as for military members, the sick, and those traveling out of state during the election cycle. However, the bill currently languishes in the Senate due to a lack of Republican support.
Democrats sold mail-in voting on a massive scale in 2020 to a frightened public under the banner of public health. They quickly found they liked the electoral edge that came with it, so they made it a permanent demand. Meanwhile, a compliant press insisted that any voter who wanted to cast a ballot in person the old-fashioned way was endangering his neighbors. Americans accepted this the same way they accepted school closures, mask mandates for toddlers, and vaccine passports for restaurants.
The mass psychosis that led to this obedience has given way since that infamous year. Mail-in voting is simply the last to go. As the memory of COVID-19 recedes, even Democratic voters are drifting back toward normalcyâshowing up, marking a ballot, and going home, the way Americans did for two centuries before 2020. Left alone, that drift will likely continue through the rest of this decade, and by the 2030s, mail-in voting will be no more common than it was in the 2010s.
But Republicans don't have to wait for normalcy to run its course. They can course-correct now with little resistance. The SAVE America Act would put safeguards around mail-in voting by requiring voter ID. And, if a Senate version like Schmitt's passes, it would convert no-excuse mail-in voting back into a needs-based system for those with a genuine reason they can't appear in person.
The United States is on the mend from the political side effects of COVID-19. It's time to speed-run a full recovery on the electoral front. Americans can contact their senator today atÂ SaveActNow.com Â and demand that they force a vote on it.

American officials increasingly believe China is unlikely to attack Taiwan before 2028, despite President Xi Jinping ordering his military to be able to seize the island by force by 2027, according to sources familiar with Washington's assessments.
China's military readiness has been hampered by Xi's sweeping anti-corruption purge, while Beijing may also want to see the outcome of Taiwan's 2028 presidential election before deciding its next move, two serving US officials, a former official and another person familiar with the matter said.
But the risk of military action could rise significantly if Taiwan's ruling Democratic Progressive Party wins an unprecedented fourth consecutive presidential term, particularly if President Lai Ching-te is reelected.
"If that happens, I think 2028 becomes pretty sporty," one US official said.
Lai and the DPP champion Taiwan's separate identity, angering Beijing, which considers the self-governed island part of its territory. Taiwan rejects China's sovereignty claims and says its people can decide its future.
The assessment marks a shift from concerns about 2027, when Xi ordered the People's Liberation Army to be capable of taking Taiwan by force. US officials have long viewed the date, which marks the PLA's centenary, as a military readiness target rather than a firm invasion deadline.
Beijing has never publicly acknowledged plans to attack Taiwan in 2027 and continues to say it favors peaceful "reunification," while refusing to renounce the use of force.
US intelligence agencies have also previously identified signs of caution. In their annual threat assessment in March, they said Beijing had no fixed timeline for invading Taiwan and continued to prefer taking control of the island without war if possible.
The Pentagon declined to comment. The Chinese Embassy in Washington and Taiwan's representative office did not immediately respond to requests for comment.
Washington remains Taipei's primary global benefactor and defense vendor despite lacking official diplomatic relations, though American officials provided varying views regarding how heavily Beijing might weigh the outcome of the 2028 U.S. presidential election when evaluating potential military maneuvers.
Although three sources said Chinese strategists might want to gauge the U.S. political outcome—especially amid waning public enthusiasm in America for overseas military engagements—the primary U.S. official emphasized that Beijing considers both Democratic and Republican parties essentially unified in their firm backing of Taiwan.
While Chinese leadership might prefer a certain outcome in the 2028 American vote, "it doesn't become as decisive a factor in my opinion, as it might have been 15 years ago," the official said.
President Donald Trump has consistently minimized the threat of an imminent Chinese assault on Taiwan under his watch, claiming publicly last year that Xi personally assured him Beijing would abstain from invading while he remained in power.
Trump offered brief remarks on Taiwan after his bilateral meeting with Xi in Washington last week, confirming only that Taiwan came up during their exchange and that Xi fully understood his stance.
Beijing repeatedly describes Taiwan as its paramount political priority and a non-negotiable matter touching upon sovereign integrity.
China has persistently demanded a complete halt to American military aid to Taiwan. Following his May visit to Beijing, Trump suspended approval of an approximate $14 billion arms deal, characterizing the military assistance package as a leverage tool or "negotiating chip."
Decades of American policy have concentrated on bolstering Taiwan's defensive capacity, enabling the island to withstand an initial Chinese offensive until Washington and partner nations can intervene defensively.
Chinese leader Xi has not formally abandoned his directive ordering the People's Liberation Army to possess full operational capability to seize Taiwan by force next year, officials noted.
However, the armed forces failed to meet their target operational benchmarks over the past year because Beijing's extensive anti-corruption sweep disrupted progress, sources explained.
Since assuming power in 2012, Xi has spearheaded an uncompromising campaign targeting corruption and party disloyalty. Millions of bureaucrats across China's state apparatus have faced investigation, resulting in the downfall and removal of numerous high-ranking party leaders, officials, and commanders.
Recently, the People's Liberation Army became a primary focus of this internal purge. A wave of high-level inquiries and dismissals leaves only two active members on the once seven-person Central Military Commission, including Xi, who remains chair.
Chinese military maneuvers last year were visibly smaller in scale and less aggressive than in previous periods, according to the U.S. official. Although drills expanded somewhat this year, the official indicated top Chinese military commanders remained privately dissatisfied with force readiness levels.
The official noted Beijing appears to have extracted critical insights from recent conflicts in Iran and Ukraine, realizing that an invasion requires immediate, overwhelming success to prevent becoming entangled in an exhausting, prolonged war of attrition.
Significant operational hurdles remain unaddressed.
"There are way too many pieces that aren't quite in place yet for what would be the most difficult military operation any military has attempted probably since the Allied invasion of Normandy," the official said.

articles.title_orig: Russia launches massive strikes on Ukraine’s energy grid, forcing power cuts ahead of winter
articles.title_zh: Russia launches massive strikes on Ukraine’s energy grid, forcing power cuts ahead of winter
articles.content_orig:
Russia has launched a widely anticipated attack on Ukraine's power grid, hitting key facilities in Kyiv and other major cities across the country, marking one of the biggest energy assaults in months.
Ukrainian officials and national security experts have been warning about the prospect of a Russian air campaign on its energy infrastructure ahead of winter, fearing another extremely difficult cold snap at a time when the country faces an acute air defense shortage.
Seven people were killed in the latest attacks, officials said Wednesday, with state grid power operator Ukrenergo imposing emergency power cuts in Kyiv and three other regions. Freezing temperatures have been forecast at night in Ukraine's capital over the coming days.
"Russia has launched massive strikes on energy infrastructure," Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhii Koretskyi said Wednesday via Telegram.
"Since the summer, there has been practically no day when the enemy has not attacked energy infrastructure. But such a massive and combined attack has occurred for the first time since the end of the last heating season," Koretskyi said, according to a translation.
Russia's Ministry of Defense said Wednesday that it had delivered a "massive strike" by ground-based high-precision weapons and attack drones at a communication center in Kyiv, as well as Ukraine's energy system facilities and the port infrastructure of Izmail in southwestern part of the Odesa region.
The ministry had said in late August that it was preparing a bombardment of Ukraine's energy infrastructure as part of Russia's response to Ukrainian attacks on its fuel and energy facilities.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy warned Russian President Vladimir Putin at the United Nations General Assembly last week that Kyiv would make winter deeply painful for Russia if the two sides were unable to agree to an energy truce.
"Ukrainians understand that this winter could be very harsh for us. But in response, we will have no choice but to make it painful for Russia too," Zelenskyy said on Sept. 23.
U.S. President Donald Trump claimed that Russia and Moscow had agreed to halt attacks on energy facilities last month, although both nations swiftly clarified that no formal deal had been finalized.
Trump has also previously urged Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian oil refineries, saying the attacks are "hurting the world" as fuel supply disruptions continue to prop up U.S. diesel prices .
Earlier this week, NATO condemned Russia's nuclear threats after publicly acknowledging a tense exchange with Moscow.
The Russian Embassy in Belgium had accused the alliance of escalating the situation around Kaliningrad, a small Russian exclave on the Baltic Sea, between NATO member states Poland and Lithuania.
The embassy said NATO's "reckless and irresponsible" approach to Kaliningrad heightens the risk of a direct military confrontation.
It added that Moscow was ready to use its entire military arsenal if NATO tried to block the region, according to Russian state news agency Tass.
Matthew Whitaker, the U.S. ambassador to NATO, said that the alliance was prepared for whatever action Russia may take against a NATO country.
"What we have been very clear in communicating back to the Russian side is that we are a defensive alliance. We will defend every inch of NATO territory but at the same time we are not offensive orientated," Whitaker told CNBC's "Squawk Box Europe" on Thursday.
"This is, you know, a situation where because of the lack of success on the battlefield in Ukraine, I think Russia is trying to lash out, but ultimately ... we are prepared," he added.

articles.title_zh: Box Office: ‘Verity’ Aims for $35 Million Debut and Anne Hathaway’s Third No. 1 Movie of the Year, ‘Digger’ Could Bomb With $12 Million
articles.content_orig:
Senior Film and Media Reporter
Anne Hathaway is returning to a familiar spot — the top of box office charts — as “ Verity ” hits the big screen over the weekend. The adaptation of Colleen Hoover’s bestseller is targeting a solid domestic debut of $30 million to $35 million from 3,510 theaters, which should be enough to register as Hathaway’s third No. 1 opening of the year. She also starred in this summer’s blockbusters “The Devil Wears Prada 2″ and “The Odyssey.”
In a twist that few might have predicted this time last year, “Verity” will tower over Tom Cruise and Alejandro González Iñárritu’s R-rated environmental satire “ Digger ,” which also debuts this weekend. The big-budget film is shaping up to be one of the year’s biggest bombs , with opening weekend projections of $12 million to $15 million from 3,300 North American screens.
“Verity” is the latest of Hoover’s works to get the big-screen treatment following Sony’s 2024 sleeper hit “It Ends With Us,” Paramount’s 2025 drama “Regretting You” and Universal’s 2026 romance “Reminders of Him.” Among her adaptations, “It Ends With Us” landed the biggest debut with $50 million, followed by “Reminders of Him” with $17 million and “Regretting You” with $13.6 million. “It Ends With Us” is the highest-grossing of the trio by far with $350 million globally. Hoover’s film adaptations have modest budgets, making them low-risk bets for studios.
“Verity” was produced for $40 million and will help Amazon MGM rebound after this summer’s “Masters of the Universe,” which flopped with $113 million globally against a $200 million budget. Amazon MGM, a relative newcomer to theatrical, delivered its first major win in the spring with Ryan Gosling’s astronaut drama “Project Hail Mary,” which grossed $684 million globally. Later this year, the studio has “I Play Rocky,” a crowd pleaser about the making of the 1976 Sylvester Stallone classic “Rocky,” and the heist thriller “How to Rob a Bank” with Nicholas Hoult and Pete Davidson.
Hathaway, who also starred in this year’s psychodrama “Mother Mary” and sci-fi thriller “The End of Oak Street,” shares the screen in “Verity” with Dakota Johnson and Josh Hartnett. Directed by Michael Showalter (“The Big Sick”), the movie centers around famed author Verity Crawford, who gets badly injured in a car accident, leaving her husband to hire a struggling writer to complete the remaining books in the popular series. Reviews have been mixed, with Variety’s Guy Lodge calling “Verity” a “listless” and “unintentionally funny tale.”
“Digger” looks to continue a dismal year for Warner Bros. — having fielded such misfires as “The Bride!” and “Supergirl” — and the timing couldn’t be worse. Paramount’s acquisition of Warner Bros. is set to close next week . For Warners, it’s a stark reversal in fortunes from the studio’s 2025 slate, which boasted an unprecedented string of commercial triumphs including “Sinners,” “A Minecraft Movie” and “Weapons.”
“Digger” was greenlit at Warner Bros. for $125 million, but according to four knowledgeable sources, the budget climbed to $160 million to $180 million after production went over schedule. A Warner Bros. spokesperson disputes those figures. Box office experts say a movie of this size would need a debut near $40 million to justify its price tag.
Cruise stars in “Digger” as a wealthy oil tycoon whose company causes a potential catastrophe. Reviews and word-of-mouth have been so negative that Warner Bros. has started to embrace the bad press . In a new ad, the studio told moviegoers to “decide for yourself” after critics bashed the movie as “unpleasant” and “baffling.”

On Joshua’s rise to stardom: “During the time when AJ become world champion, I was getting drunk every day and taking cocaine every week. I mostly find myself defending my arch rival to fans I meet on the street. I say to them, if you could achieve 10 percent of what this man’s achieved, you’d be fuckin’ doing well. That aside, obviously, we’re here to fight, and fight we will. I’m looking forward to the challenge. It’s been 10 years in the making. We’ve both had our ups and downs, and finally, we’re arrived at this moment. I’m 38, AJ’s 37 or will be 37 soon. People say, ‘Is it too late?’ Is it fucking too late? It’s the icing on the cake of two great careers, to throw down in front of 80,000 people, and may the best man win. Let’s go out fuckin’ swinging.”

On being in Britain’s biggest fight ever: “I wouldn’t have it any other way. There’s been some brilliant fights in this country, and in the biggest division, the glory division of the heavyweights, this is the biggest of today. I don’t believe in comparing different eras and different times together, we can only be the biggest of our generation and our time. Me and AJ’s gonna go there and throw down. It’s just an unbelievable event, because it’s been simmering nicely for about a decade and a half. It’s been an unbelievable journey having both of us together, both coming from the same country, both going out there and dominating, winning world championships and beating all the comers. We’ve had our ups and downs, you’ve all seen it live on TV. Finally now, towards the end of it all, we get to fight each other on the world’s biggest stage, with the world’s biggest broadcaster, and everybody’s gonna be there. And everybody’s gonna want to be there anymore. … As a boxing fan, which I am, this is the one that I would want to see more than any other fight in the world today. There isn’t a fight out there that can even come close to the excitement and what’s gonna happen, the build-up, everything. It’s just a whole event, a global event, where everybody can watch it.”
On being born to fight: “From a little kid, it’s all I ever wanted to do was be a fighter, be a world champion. I got the opportunity and I seized the moment. I was the most unlikely child to be a champion — fat, awkward, gangly, all of the above. I never let anybody dissuade me on ‘you can’t do this, you can’t do that,’ yada yada yada. I always pushed through when the odds were stacked against me, for many different reasons.”
On the differences in their builds: “I’m just living proof that if you believe in yourself, and you work hard and dedicate yourself to something, then no matter what you look like, what build you are, what background you come from, you can achieve anything. I stand here today as the most awkwardly built world heavyweight champion in the history of sport. I’m a bald, fat, bearded, ugly, slow, ponderous, all of the above, whatever people want to say. But at the end of the day, I get shit done. And then you got this guy here, he’s carved in stone like he’s made of marble, and every time he gets cracked on the jaw, he falls over. That’s also true! … When I crack him on the jaw with a right hand, he’s gonna go down like a sack of shit.”
On how he feels physically: “God is good! I feel fresh, I feel very excited about this opportunity to work again. … I’m happy. Honestly, I’m grateful.”
On how he responds to big pressure: “I don’t know what it is, I’ve just got something in me. I just can do what I do. When I walked in the gym when I was 18 years old, three years later I was fighting for Great Britain in the Olympics. I turned pro, three years later I was world champion. It’s just what I do. It’s not complicated. I don’t find (boxing) too complicated, it’s pretty straightforward. It’s spirit vs spirit, it’s just man vs man, and the best man will win.”

I trained for Ngannou like I did with every other fighter, same way Fury did. There are comparisons in fights, of course, but me and (Fury) haven’t stepped in the ring. So I can’t say I’m gonna do this, because he done this to this fighter, and I done that to that fighter, because we haven’t stepped in the ring yet.”
